---
title: "Logistic Regression"
body-classes: fam-linear
---

[**Linear family**]{.fam-badge} · the default first classifier for a binary target, and the linear-boundary baseline every other classifier is judged against. It is the classification analogue of [OLS](ols.qmd) — same linear machinery, aimed at a probability instead of a continuous number. Siblings: [LDA](lda.qmd) (also a linear boundary, but assumes Gaussian classes with shared covariance), [Adaline](adaline.qmd) (the *same* gradient-descent update, with MSE + linear activation instead of cross-entropy + sigmoid), [kNN](knn.qmd) and [Decision Trees](decision_trees.qmd) (non-parametric, non-linear alternatives).

## 1. Essence

Logistic regression predicts the **probability** that an observation belongs to the positive class. It does so with the same linear core as [OLS](ols.qmd) — one coefficient per predictor plus an intercept, combined into a single number $z = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p$ (the *net input*) — but then passes that number through the **sigmoid** function $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$, which squashes any real value into $[0,1]$ so it can be read as a probability (Lecture 4, slide 7/11). To turn a probability into a class label you apply a **threshold**, by default $0.5$: predict class 1 when $\sigma(z) \ge 0.5$, else class 0 (Lecture 8, slide 24/29). Despite the name, it is a **classification** technique, not a regression one (notebook `06_Logistic_regression.ipynb`, cell 1).

The reason the linear-plus-sigmoid form is natural, not arbitrary, is that it makes the **log-odds linear** in the predictors: $\log\!\big(\pi/(1-\pi)\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p$, where $\pi$ is the probability of the positive class (Lecture 4, slide 6/11; *the course slides and notebooks write this probability as $p$ — here we use $\pi$ to avoid colliding with $p$ = number of predictors, see the [notation table](../appendix/notation_table.qmd)*). This gives each coefficient a clean reading: a one-unit increase in $z$ multiplies the **odds** $\pi/(1-\pi)$ by $e \approx 2.718$ (Lecture 4, slide 8/11). That interpretability — coefficients as effects on the log-odds — is the whole appeal, the same way it is for OLS.

It is a **parametric** model fit by **maximum likelihood** (equivalently, by minimizing the negative log-likelihood, i.e. the **cross-entropy** loss). Compared with its nearest neighbors: [LDA](lda.qmd) draws a linear boundary too but gets there by modelling each class as Gaussian with a shared covariance — logistic regression makes no distributional assumption about the predictors and estimates the boundary directly; [Adaline](adaline.qmd) is the *identical* gradient-descent learner with the sigmoid swapped for a linear activation and cross-entropy swapped for MSE (Lecture 8, slides 27–28/29); and [kNN](knn.qmd) and [trees](decision_trees.qmd) drop the linear-boundary assumption entirely.

## 2. When to use / when *not* to use

::: {.callout-intuition}
**Reach for logistic regression when…**

- The target is a **class** (binary first; multi-class via One-vs-All or softmax) and you want **calibrated probabilities**, not just a hard label — e.g. "chance of survival", "chance of disease" (Lecture 8, slide 24/29).
- You want **interpretable coefficients**: each $\beta_j$ is the change in log-odds per unit of $x_j$, and $e^{\beta_j}$ is the odds multiplier — the classification counterpart of reading OLS slopes.
- You expect a roughly **linear decision boundary** in the feature space (or one you can linearize with transforms/interactions).
- You need a **fast, transparent baseline** before reaching for trees or neural nets. It is a natural candidate classifier for the Spring-2025 exam's classification task (see §7).
:::

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Reach for something else when…**

- **The classes are well-separated Gaussians with similar covariance** → [**LDA**](lda.qmd) uses that structure and can be more stable, especially with little data or perfectly separable classes (where plain logistic regression's coefficients can diverge). Lecture 4 (slide 4/11) lists LDA's assumptions explicitly.
- **The boundary is clearly non-linear** and you don't want to hand-engineer the form → [**Decision Trees / Random Forests**](random_forests.qmd) (axis-aligned splits) or [**kNN**](knn.qmd) capture curvature automatically.
- **You want raw flexibility / a stepping stone to neural nets** → a single sigmoid unit *is* logistic regression; stacking them gives an [**MLP**](nn_basics.qmd). [Adaline](adaline.qmd) is the same learner with a linear output.
- **Predictors heavily outnumber observations or are strongly correlated** → coefficients become unstable; use the built-in L2/L1 penalty (the `C`/`penalty` arguments, §3) — the classification echo of [Ridge/Lasso](regularization.qmd).
:::

## 3. Code idiom

The canonical course idiom is `scikit-learn`'s `LogisticRegression` (notebook 06, on Titanic); the course also builds the model **from scratch** by gradient descent (notebook 15, on Iris) to show the sigmoid + cross-entropy mechanics — and to make the [Adaline](adaline.qmd) → logistic link concrete.

**Canonical (sklearn)** — *(notebook `06_Logistic_regression.ipynb`, cell 7)*

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

log_reg = LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs', max_iter=500)  # lbfgs = quasi-Newton optimizer
log_reg.fit(X_train, y_train)                                # X: (n_samples, n_features), y in {0,1}
log_reg.predict(X_test)                                      # hard labels at the 0.5 threshold
log_reg.predict_proba(X_test)                                # [P(class 0), P(class 1)] per row
log_reg.coef_        # the log-odds slopes β₁…β_p
log_reg.intercept_   # the intercept β₀
```

`solver='lbfgs'` is the optimizer (a quasi-Newton method); `max_iter=500` raises the iteration cap from the `default` 100 so the optimizer converges on this data. Everything else is `default`: `penalty='l2'`, `C=1.0` (inverse regularization strength — *smaller* `C` means *stronger* shrinkage, the classification analogue of a larger Ridge `alpha`), `class_weight=None`. For imbalanced classes, `class_weight='balanced'` and tuning `C`/`penalty` are the standard knobs (real sklearn parameters; values left `default` as they are not changed in the notebook).

**From scratch — gradient descent** *(notebook `15_LogisticRegression.ipynb`, cell id `a342d4e2`)*. This is [Adaline](adaline.qmd) with two changes: a **sigmoid** activation and a **cross-entropy** loss. Per Lecture 8 (slides 27–28/29) the gradient-descent *update* is unchanged — both reduce to $-\tfrac1n\sum(y-\text{activation})\,x_j$ — only the activation inside differs ([disagreements R9-11]):

```python
class LogisticRegressionGD:
    def __init__(self, eta=0.01, n_iter=50, random_state=1):   # course uses eta=0.3, n_iter=1000
        self.eta = eta; self.n_iter = n_iter; self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(self, X, y):
        rgen = np.random.RandomState(self.random_state)
        self.w_ = rgen.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.01, size=X.shape[1])  # small random init
        self.b_ = 0.0
        self.losses_ = []
        for i in range(self.n_iter):
            output = self.activation(self.net_input(X))      # σ(z), the predicted probability
            errors = (y - output)                            # y − σ(z)
            self.w_ += self.eta * X.T.dot(errors) / X.shape[0]   # vectorized GD step (÷ n)
            self.b_ += self.eta * errors.mean()
            output_clipped = np.clip(output, 1e-10, 1.0 - 1e-10)         # avoid log(0)
            loss = -y.dot(np.log(output_clipped)) - (1 - y).dot(np.log(1 - output_clipped))
            self.losses_.append(loss / X.shape[0])           # binary cross-entropy per sample

    def net_input(self, X):   return np.dot(X, self.w_) + self.b_       # z = w·x + b
    def activation(self, z):  return 1. / (1. + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -250, 250)))  # sigmoid (clipped)
    def predict(self, X):     return np.where(self.activation(self.net_input(X)) >= 0.5, 1, 0)
```

The course instantiates this with `LogisticRegressionGD(eta=0.3, n_iter=1000, random_state=1)` (cell id `50ee34c8`) — a learning rate `eta` ($\eta$) of `0.3` and `n_iter` `1000` epochs, well above the class defaults `eta=0.01, n_iter=50`.

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Idiom variation worth knowing — multi-class via One-vs-All.** For 3 classes the from-scratch notebook trains one binary detector per class and stacks their sigmoid outputs, then takes the `argmax` *(notebook `15_LogisticRegression.ipynb`, cell id `f4432549`)*:

```python
probabilities = np.zeros((X.shape[0], 3))
for k in range(3):
    y_k = np.where(y_all == k, 1, 0)                 # class k vs the rest
    lrgd_k = LogisticRegressionGD(eta=0.3, n_iter=1000, random_state=1).fit(X, y_k)
    probabilities[:, k] = lrgd_k.activation(lrgd_k.net_input(X))
predicted = np.argmax(probabilities, axis=1)         # pick the most confident detector
```

The notebook explicitly warns these three sigmoid outputs **do not sum to 1** — each is an independent binary detector; for true probabilities that sum to 1 you would use **softmax (multinomial) regression** instead (cell id `6b3b3496`). sklearn's `LogisticRegression` does softmax/OvA automatically when `y` has more than two classes.
:::

## 4. Worked examples

### Example 1 — Titanic survival with sklearn {#sec-logistic-titanic}

The course's canonical example predicts survival on the **Titanic** training set *(notebook `06_Logistic_regression.ipynb`, cells 3–11)*. After `dropna()` the 891-row frame collapses to **183 rows** (the sparse `Cabin` column drives most of the loss, biasing the sample toward 1st-class passengers — a real data quirk the notebook does not flag), `Sex` is encoded male=1/female=0, and six features are used with an 80/20 split (`random_state=15`):

```python
df = pd.read_csv('../data/titanic/train.csv').dropna()        # 891 → 183 rows
df['Sex'] = df['Sex'].apply(lambda x: 1 if x == 'male' else 0)
X = df[['Pclass', 'Sex', 'Age', 'SibSp', 'Parch', 'Fare']]
y = df['Survived']
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=15)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs', max_iter=500).fit(X_train, y_train)
```

This yields **test accuracy ≈ 0.892** (33/37 correct), well above the **majority-class baseline of 0.459** (always predict "did not survive") — *(computed via the course venv, `random_state=15`; the notebook stores no outputs)*. The confusion matrix is `[[13, 4], [0, 20]]`: every actual survivor is caught (recall 1.00 for class 1) at the cost of 4 false alarms (class-0 recall 0.76). The fitted coefficients read directly as log-odds effects:

| Feature | `Pclass` | `Sex` (male=1) | `Age` | `SibSp` | `Parch` | `Fare` | Intercept |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\beta$ | −0.33 | **−2.14** | −0.02 | +0.14 | −0.24 | +0.002 | +3.25 |

*(computed, same run.)* The dominant effect is `Sex`: being male carries $\beta \approx -2.14$, so it **multiplies the odds of survival by $e^{-2.14} \approx 0.12$** versus female — the "women first" pattern, read straight off the coefficient via the odds interpretation of Lecture 4 (slide 8/11). `Pclass` is negative (higher class number = lower class = lower survival odds), as expected.

### Example 2 — predicting a probability (synthetic) {#sec-logistic-proba}

A minimal demo shows that the model's output really is the sigmoid's probability *(notebook `06_Logistic_regression.ipynb`, cell 14)*. Four points lie on a perfectly separable line (`y=0` for the first two, `y=1` for the last two); a new point `[5, 10]` extends the `y=1` side:

```python
X_synth = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4], [3, 6], [4, 8]]); y_synth = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
clf = LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs').fit(X_synth, y_synth)
clf.predict_proba([[5, 10]])    # → [[0.0063, 0.9937]]
clf.predict([[5, 10]])          # → [1]
```

The model returns **P(class 1) ≈ 0.994** *(computed via venv; the notebook stores no output)* — high confidence, because the point sits firmly on the positive side of the boundary. This is `predict_proba` exposing $\sigma(z)$ directly; `predict` is just that value thresholded at 0.5.

### Example 3 — from-scratch GD and One-vs-All on Iris {#sec-logistic-iris}

The from-scratch `LogisticRegressionGD` is fit on Iris *(notebook `15_LogisticRegression.ipynb`)*. On the binary problem (first 100 rows, Setosa vs Versicolor, sepal+petal length), with `eta=0.3, n_iter=1000`, the cross-entropy loss falls from **≈ 0.69** (the $-\ln 0.5$ of a random start) to **≈ 0.006**, reaching **100% training accuracy** — these two classes are linearly separable, so the GD learner drives the loss almost to zero *(computed via venv, `random_state=1`; the notebook stores no outputs)*. Extending to all four features (Example 2 in the notebook) also gives **100% training accuracy**.

The 3-class **One-vs-All** extension (cell id `f4432549`) trains three detectors on all 150 rows and takes the `argmax`, giving **overall training accuracy ≈ 0.91** *(computed, same run)*. The errors concentrate where Versicolor and Virginica overlap: per-class recall is 1.00 (Setosa), 0.98 (Versicolor), but only **0.74 (Virginica)** — the limit of a *linear* boundary on classes that are not linearly separable, exactly the case where you would reach for [kNN](knn.qmd) or a [tree](decision_trees.qmd).

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
The Titanic example uses `dropna()` on the full frame, which silently discards 79% of rows — a reminder that preprocessing choices can matter more than the model. See the [classification showdown](../cross_method/showdowns.qmd) for logistic vs LDA vs kNN vs tree on a shared 2-feature boundary.
:::

## 5. Visualization

The sigmoid is the one picture that earns its place: it shows *why* a linear $z$ becomes a probability. The figure below plots $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ — flat near 0 and 1, steepest at $z=0$ where $\sigma(0)=0.5$ (the decision threshold). Static prose can state "the sigmoid squashes $\mathbb{R}$ into $[0,1]$"; only the curve shows the S-shape and where the 0.5 cut falls.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-logistic-sigmoid
//| fig-cap: "The logistic sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) mapping the net input z (the OLS-style linear combination β₀+β₁x₁+…) into a probability in [0,1]. The curve is flat in the tails and steepest at z=0, where σ(0)=0.5 — the default classification threshold (dashed). A passenger with z>0 is predicted to survive; z<0, not. The odds π/(1−π) double-and-then-some (×e≈2.718) for every +1 in z."
famLinear = (getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--family-linear').trim() || "#2E86AB")
sigmoidData = {
  const sig = z => 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-z));
  return d3.range(-8, 8.01, 0.1).map(z => ({z, p: sig(z)}));
}
Plot.plot({
  height: 300, marginLeft: 50, grid: true,
  x: {label: "z = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … (net input)", domain: [-8, 8]},
  y: {label: "σ(z) = P(class 1)", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#ddd"}),
    Plot.dot([{z: 0, p: 0.5}], {x: "z", y: "p", fill: "#2e8b57", r: 4}),
    Plot.text([{z: 0, p: 0.5}], {x: "z", y: "p", text: ["σ(0)=0.5"], dx: 38, dy: -8, fill: "#2e8b57"}),
    Plot.line(sigmoidData, {x: "z", y: "p", stroke: famLinear, strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})
```

## 6. Diagnostics & interpretation

What to report and look at to decide whether a logistic model is working:

- **Accuracy vs a baseline** — compare against the **majority-class** rate (Titanic: 0.892 vs 0.459). Accuracy alone is misleading on **imbalanced** data, so also report the confusion matrix.
- **Confusion matrix + classification report** — precision, recall, F1 per class *(notebook 06, cell 11)*. These expose *where* errors fall (the Titanic model trades false positives for perfect survivor recall). On imbalanced problems these matter more than accuracy.
- **Coefficients as log-odds / odds ratios** — read the sign and magnitude of each $\beta_j$; $e^{\beta_j}$ is the odds multiplier per unit. As with [OLS](ols.qmd), only compare magnitudes after checking feature scale, and watch for sign flips from correlated predictors.
- **Threshold tuning** — the 0.5 cut is a default, not a law. Lower it (e.g. 0.3) to catch more positives at the cost of more false alarms; raise it (0.7) for the reverse. The notebook leaves this as an exercise (cell 12).
- **Probability calibration** — `predict_proba` gives probabilities; check they are sensible (well-separated data pushes them toward 0/1, as in the synthetic example's 0.994).

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
Comparative diagnostic vs siblings: logistic regression gives you *coefficients as odds ratios* (interpretable effect sizes) where [LDA](lda.qmd) gives you *class means and a shared covariance* (a generative story), and a [Random Forest](random_forests.qmd) gives *feature importances* (rankings, not "+1 unit ⇒ ×e odds"). All three can draw similar boundaries on separable data; choose the one whose output answers your question. Logistic and LDA are *both linear* — they differ in assumptions, not in boundary shape.
:::

## 7. Past-exam lens

::: {.callout-exam}
**How logistic regression shows up.** It is a **candidate classifier for the Spring-2025 take-home's classification task (Assignment 4)**, alongside [kNN](knn.qmd), [trees](decision_trees.qmd), and others (`phase0/concept_inventory.md`). Expect to (i) write the `LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs', max_iter=500)` idiom from §3, (ii) report **accuracy plus the confusion matrix / classification report** against a sensible baseline, and (iii) **interpret the coefficients as log-odds / odds ratios** — the grade rests on the justification, e.g. explaining the dominant `Sex` effect via the odds interpretation, at least as much as on the code. The from-scratch GD version (notebook 15) and the [Adaline](adaline.qmd) link (Lecture 8) are theory the exam can probe conceptually ("how is logistic regression obtained from Adaline?" → swap MSE→cross-entropy, linear→sigmoid; the GD step is unchanged). Logistic regression has not appeared as a stand-alone derivation question; it appears as a classification baseline.
:::

## 8. Math {#sec-logistic-math}

::: {.math-section}
::: {.math-off-hint}
*Math is off. Use the **Math** toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and "full" for the rigorous version).*
:::

::: {.callout-math-a}
**Mode A — course level.** *(written in Phase 3)* — the log-odds linear form $\log\!\big(\pi/(1-\pi)\big) = \beta_0 + \sum_j \beta_j x_j$ and its inversion to the sigmoid $\pi = \sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ (Lecture 4, slides 6–8/11; notebook 06, cell 1); the binary **cross-entropy** loss $L = -\tfrac1n\sum_i [\,y_i\log\sigma(z_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\sigma(z_i))\,]$ (Lecture 8, slide 25/29); and the **gradient-descent update** $w_j \leftarrow w_j + \eta\cdot\tfrac1n\sum_i (y_i - \sigma(z_i))\,x_{ij}$ (Lecture 8, slide 28/29; notebook 15, cell id `a342d4e2`), with the interpretation of each term. See the [math appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-gd).
:::

::: {.callout-math-b}
**Mode B — full rigor.** *(written in Phase 3)* — the **maximum-likelihood** derivation (Bernoulli likelihood ⇒ negative log-likelihood = cross-entropy ⇒ no closed form, hence iterative optimization), and the proof that the [Adaline](adaline.qmd)→logistic **gradient step is identical** despite the change of activation and loss [disagreements R9-11] (Lecture 8, slides 27–28/29, the course's "optional home exercise"). Anchored to ESL §4.4 (logistic regression / cross-entropy) and the [maximum-likelihood appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-mle).
:::
:::
